items.topic: Trend adjustment in weather derivative temperature modeling
items.definition: A modeling choice for weather derivatives in which historical temperature data is corrected for an apparent long-term warming or cooling drift before being used to estimate expected future temperatures, with the year the adjustment calculation begins being a separate and consequential choice.
items.core_idea: Because no single objectively correct historical average temperature exists, analysts must decide whether to detrend the temperature history, and if so, from what starting year — and that starting-year choice alone can swing the resulting trend meaningfully.
key_points: There is no historically observable 'true' average temperature for a location, so valuing or trading weather derivatives requires the analyst to make explicit modeling assumptions.
Trend adjustment is one such assumption: deciding whether to correct the historical temperature series for a long-term trend before using it as a baseline.
If trend adjustment is used, the choice of starting year for the calculation is itself a second important decision, since it can change the outcome substantially.
In the Paris temperature example, beginning the trend calculation in 1958 (an unusually warm year) produces a different trend result than beginning it in 1963 (an unusually cold year).
relationships: Paired with the data truncation decision as one of two key modeling assumptions for weather derivatives
trading_implications: Different reasonable choices of trend start-year can produce materially different expected-temperature baselines and therefore different valuations for the same weather derivative contract.
Traders/valuers should be aware of which start year a counterparty's or vendor's model uses, and consider testing sensitivity to that choice.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming there is one objective, agreed-upon historical average temperature to model against.
Treating the trend start year as a neutral technical detail rather than a assumption that can swing results.

items.topic: Data truncation in weather derivative temperature modeling
items.definition: A modeling decision about how many years of historical temperature data to include when building the baseline used to value or trade weather derivatives.
items.core_idea: Visual inspection of long temperature records suggests the data alternates between multi-year stretches of relatively stable temperatures and stretches where temperatures are trending, implying older data may be less representative of current conditions and supporting the case for using a shorter, more recent data window.
key_points: Besides trend adjustment, analysts must separately decide the length of the historical data set used to model temperature.

Visual inspection of historical records (illustrated with the Paris annual average temperature figure) shows apparent multi-year periods of stable temperatures alternating with periods of trending temperatures.

This pattern raises the possibility that older data in the series is less predictive of current/future temperatures than more recent data, which is a rationale for truncating (shortening) the data set used.
relationships: Paired with the trend adjustment decision as one of two key modeling assumptions for weather derivatives
trading_implications: Using a shorter, more recent data window versus the full historical record changes the modeled expected temperature baseline and therefore the fair value assigned to a weather derivative.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming that including more historical data always produces a more accurate model, rather than recognizing older data may be less representative if the climate/period has structurally shifted.
